overview: Pentaceratops sternbergii ("five-horned face") was a chasmosaurine ceratopsid from the Campanian of New Mexico (~76 Ma), named for what appeared to be five horns: the nasal horn, two brow horns, and two elongated cheek horns (epijugals). Its skull with frill — reaching an estimated 3 metres in length — rivals Torosaurus for the largest ceratopsid skull ever, though the frill is fully open to debate regarding preservation.

As a southern North American chasmosaurine, Pentaceratops fills an important biogeographic gap: its large body size and elaborate frill help document how chasmosaurine horn and frill complexity evolved between the earlier Chasmosaurus of Alberta and the later Triceratops of the same region, providing a morphological bridge in the lineage.

fossilSites.name: Fruitland and Kirtland Formations
fossilSites.region: San Juan Basin, New Mexico, USA
fossilSites.note: Late Campanian continental deposits with the best-known Pentaceratops material including multiple skulls.

articles.title: Discovery and the five horns
articles.body: Named by Osborn in 1923 from Sternberg's New Mexico material. The "five horns" are the nasal horn, paired brow horns, and paired elongated epijugals (cheek projections). Strictly speaking, only the brow horns and nasal horn are true horns developed from nasal/frontal bones; the epijugals are enlarged processes of the jugal bone, present in all ceratopsids but greatly elongated in Pentaceratops.

articles.title: Frill and skull size
articles.body: A referred skull (OMNH 10165) estimated at 2.3 metres without frill and over 3 metres with frill has been cited as the largest known ceratopsid skull, though the completeness of this estimate is questioned. The frill parietal fenestrae are proportionally large, and the epiparietals (frill margin bones) are prominent.

articles.title: Southern North American Late Cretaceous
articles.body: The San Juan Basin of New Mexico preserves a diverse late Campanian fauna including hadrosaurs, ankylosaurs and various small dinosaurs. Pentaceratops is the dominant ceratopsid in this fauna, which differs in composition from the contemporaneous Dinosaur Park Formation fauna of Alberta — evidence for a biogeographic boundary (Laramidia North vs South) in Late Cretaceous North America.

fossilRecord.formations: Fruitland and Kirtland formations, New Mexico, USA
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Cretaceous forested floodplains of the American Southwest.
fossilRecord.evidence: The enormous skull with five horn points is diagnostic; skull dimensions make it among the largest skulls of any land animal.

record.mya: late Campanian, about 76-74 million years ago
record.description: Pentaceratops sternbergii was a chasmosaurine ceratopsid from the Kirtland Formation of New Mexico, known from several skulls and partial skeletons with a deep frill and long brow horns.
facts: The name refers to three true facial horns plus elongated cheek projections.
OMNH 10165, once reconstructed as a giant Pentaceratops, was proposed as Titanoceratops; that separation remains debated.
Exact frill soft tissues and horn use are unknown.

review.ageReviewNote: Secure P. sternbergii material is late Campanian Kirtland Formation, around 75.9-73.4 Ma.

sources.citation: Lehman (1993), new data on Pentaceratops sternbergii

residualUncertainty: The identity of OMNH 10165 remains disputed.
Some historical species and referrals have been reassigned.

evidence.material: Multiple partial skulls and skeletons; some referrals of disputed identity.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Do not use OMNH 10165 to define Pentaceratops size without noting the Titanoceratops debate.
evidence.summary: Pentaceratops sternbergii was a chasmosaurine ceratopsid from the Kirtland Formation of New Mexico, known from several skulls and partial skeletons with a deep frill and long brow horns.
